stemMd: A person of mass $70\ \text{kg}$ stands on a bathroom scale on the floor of a lift. The lift is travelling **downward** and is slowing down at a steady rate of $2\ \text{m/s}^2$ as it approaches a floor. Take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$. What force does the scale register?
explanationMd:
**What to notice first.** The direction of the *acceleration*, not the direction of motion, decides whether the scale reads more or less than the weight. The lift moves down but is slowing down, so its velocity (downward) is shrinking: the acceleration points **upward**.

**The steps.** Two forces act on the person: the weight $mg = 700\ \text{N}$ downward and the push of the scale $N$ upward. Newton's second law, taking up as positive:

$$N - mg = ma \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = m(g + a) = 70 \times (10 + 2) = 840\ \text{N}.$$

The scale registers the force $N$, so it reads $840\ \text{N}$.

**How to check it.** Think of the moment a descending lift brakes: you feel pressed into the floor, heavier than usual. A reading above the $700\ \text{N}$ weight agrees with that. A reading below the weight would need a downward acceleration, which happens when a lift starts moving down or slows while going up.

distractorRationale.b: Takes the acceleration as downward because the lift is moving downward, giving $70 \times (10 - 2) = 560\ \text{N}$. A lift that is slowing while going down has an upward acceleration, so the scale reads more than the weight.
distractorRationale.c: This is the weight alone, $mg = 700\ \text{N}$, which is the reading only when the lift moves at constant velocity or is at rest. Here it is decelerating.
distractorRationale.a: Computes only $ma = 70 \times 2 = 140\ \text{N}$, the net force on the person, and forgets that the scale must also support the weight.
distractorRationale.d: Confuses mass with force: $70$ is the person's mass in kilograms. A scale's push is a force, and here it is $70 \times 12 = 840\ \text{N}$.

accessibilityText: A person of mass 70 kilograms stands on a bathroom scale on the floor of a lift. The lift is travelling downward and is slowing down at a steady rate of 2 metres per second squared. Take g equal to 10 metres per second squared. What force does the scale register? The choices are 840 newtons, 560 newtons, 700 newtons, 140 newtons and 70 newtons.

provenance.notes: Original item testing Newton's second law in an accelerating frame, where the trap is reading the acceleration direction from the direction of motion. Situation and numbers invented for this bank.

review.author: tolc-i-wave8-sciences-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Moving down and slowing means acceleration is upward, 2 m/s^2, so N = m(g + a) = 70*12 = 840 N. 560 N is the speeding-down / slowing-going-up case, 700 N is rest, 140 N is ma only. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-tolci-logic-sci-run1) reached the same answer: Moving down and slowing means acceleration is upward (2 m/s^2), so N = m(g+a) = 70*12 = 840 N. 560 N takes acceleration downward; 700 N ignores it; 140 N is ma alone.]
